challenges.name: backups-restore-quiz
challenges.title: Read the restore after the bad migration
challenges.description: Three statements about the backups Rice Rocket had when a migration deleted 9,000 delivered orders at 14:05. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: A logical dump is one consistent snapshot. Ask at which moment that snapshot was taken, and what happened to the database between that moment and 14:05.
Point-in-time recovery starts from a base backup and replays WAL forward from the moment that backup started. Which files must exist, without a hole, for a target time three days back?
Think about what else the production database received after 14:05, and where the restored copy should run while you compare and copy rows.

questions.question:
The nightly backup job and the incident, both on 3 November:

```text
$ grep rice_rocket /var/log/backup.log | tail -2
2026-11-03 02:00:01 pg_dump --format=custom --file=rice_rocket-2026-11-03.dump rice_rocket
2026-11-03 02:18:44 done, 40 GB

# application log
2026-11-03 14:05:12 migration 0142_cleanup_orders: DELETE 9000
```

Statement: "Restoring `rice_rocket-2026-11-03.dump` with `pg_restore` brings the database back to just before 14:05:12, so only the bad DELETE is undone."
questions.explanation: False. pg_dump exports one consistent snapshot taken when it started (02:00). Restoring it brings back the database as it was at 02:00: every order, payment and courier update written between 02:00 and 14:05 is missing, about 12 hours of business. Getting to 14:05:11 needs point-in-time recovery: a physical base backup plus every WAL segment written since it started. The misconception is that a dump is a recovery point you can move forward.

questions.question:
The backup settings of the self-managed staging server:

```text
base backups (pg_basebackup):  every Sunday 01:00, kept 7 days
WAL archive (archive_command): kept 3 days
today: Saturday

$ ls /backup/base
2026-11-01_0100/        # Sunday, 6 days ago
$ ls /backup/wal | head -1
00000001000000B200000041   # oldest segment, written Wednesday 15:20
```

Statement: "Because the base backups are kept 7 days, the server can be restored to any point in time of the last 7 days."
questions.explanation: False. Recovery starts from a base backup and replays WAL from the moment that backup started. The only base backup started on Sunday, but WAL before Wednesday 15:20 has been deleted, so the replay cannot get from Sunday to any later point: the backup can only be restored to the moment it finished, and no time after it is reachable. The recovery window is limited by the shorter of the two retentions, and WAL must be kept at least from the start of the oldest base backup you rely on. The misconception is that each piece's retention guarantees the window on its own.

questions.question:
The team prepares point-in-time recovery for the incident:

```text
# a NEW instance restored from base backup base-2026-11-03, with WAL from the archive
restore_command = 'cp /backup/wal/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-03 14:05:11+07'
recovery_target_action = 'pause'

# application log
2026-11-03 14:05:12 migration 0142_cleanup_orders: DELETE 9000
```

Statement: "Recovering a new instance to one second before the DELETE and copying the 9,000 rows back is right; restoring the production instance itself to 14:05:11 would also throw away every order written since."
questions.explanation: True. The restored instance holds the 9,000 orders as they were just before the DELETE committed; the team copies them back into production (for example `\copy` out and an `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` in), and production keeps everything written after 14:05. `recovery_target_time` stops after the transactions that committed at or before the target, so a target of exactly 14:05:12 could replay the DELETE itself. Rolling production back in time is the last resort: it loses every write since the target. The misconception is that a restore always goes onto the damaged server.

challenges.name: restore-planner
challenges.title: Plan the point-in-time restore
challenges.description: Write the restore planner the on-call engineer runs after a bad write: given the backup catalog, the WAL archive, the commit time of the bad statement and the backup policy, it picks the base backup, the recovery target and the expected data loss and restore time, or falls back to a dump. The editor holds `restore_plan.py` with its helper functions missing, each marked by a `# [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. The rules are in the docstring: newest base backup that finished before the incident inside the retention window, a gap-free WAL chain from its start, a target one second before the incident, and a dump only when no base backup can be used.
hints: Walk the restore yourself: which base backups existed before 14:05:12, from which moment does each one need WAL, and where does the archive first stop being continuous?

The helpers are small: a filter and sort over the catalog, a loop that extends the chain only while the next segment starts at or before its current end, a `min()` for the target, and the RTO formula from the docstring.

A planner for restoring a deleted S3 object from versioned snapshots looks the same: keep the snapshots taken before the deletion and within retention, sort newest first, then walk the change log from that snapshot while it has no hole and stop just before the delete.

tests.name: The incident: PITR from this morning's base backup to one second before the DELETE
A base backup taken in panic after the incident is never the one to restore
archive_command failed 09:00-09:40: replay stops at the gap and the loss is reported
WAL missing while this morning's backup ran: that backup is skipped for an older one
No base backup inside retention: fall back to the dump and report 12 hours lost
Only a backup taken after the incident: nothing to restore from

expected.reason: no backup finished before the incident
